image_description: A group of sea lions in a turquoise pool within an enclosure. One sea lion is swimming with its head above water in the center, another is visible on the right side with just its head and upper back showing, and two others are resting on rocks on the left side. The background shows a concrete edge and some vegetation.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Head is broad with prominent sagittal crest in males.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The heads visible are wet and sleek; while broad, the specific bony sagittal crest characteristic of mature males is not clearly distinguishable due to distance, angle, and wet fur.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: External ear pinnae (visible ear flaps) distinguish from true seals.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: Small but distinct external ear flaps are visible on the central swimming sea lion and the one on the right, confirming they are otariids (sea lions/fur seals) and not phocids (true seals).
The resolution and distance make it impossible to definitively see individual whiskers, though their presence is biologically implied.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Fur is short and coarse ranging from brown to dark grey, lighter on ventral surface.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The visible fur on the animals matches the description: dark brown/grey, appearing sleek and short due to being wet.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Body exhibits streamlined fusiform form of substantial marine mammal proportions.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The bodies visible, particularly the one on the right, show the characteristic torpedo-like shape of a pinniped.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Males develop thick neck mane and are significantly larger than females.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: It is difficult to determine sex or age definitively from this distance. No obvious thick manes are visible, suggesting these may be females or juveniles, but the checkpoint cannot be fully verified as 'present' nor strictly 'absent' without closer inspection.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Foreflippers are large, broad, and hairless on underside used for terrestrial locomotion.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The animals are mostly submerged or resting on rocks where flippers are occluded by water or body position. No clear view of the foreflipper structure is available.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Hind flippers can rotate forward for walking on land.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: Hind flippers are completely submerged or occluded.
The visible portions of the animals exhibit natural biological symmetry consistent with real sea lions.

artifact_observations.reasoning: The water ripples have a slightly repetitive, patterned quality typical of AI generation, lacking the chaotic randomness of real water physics, though it is subtle.
The background elements have a 'smudged' or painterly blur that doesn't perfectly align with a standard depth-of-field effect, suggesting generative smoothing.

selected_experts.reason: To confirm the species classification and rule out misclassification as a seal or other marine mammal.
To verify the structural integrity of the head and neck connection, even if limbs are hidden.
To check for melting or fusion artifacts where the animal's body meets the water line.
To assess the realism of the water texture and lighting consistency.

Anatomical plausibility of visible head/neck structures
